R3-01.why: The HUNT phase is strong: proven hide-and-seek tension, FREEZE gives real-time cat-and-mouse with comic catches, re-hiding behind the Parent's back works well, and Snitch adds social betrayal that plays fine without voice. The mess-for-points versus mess-you-must-hide tension is a real decision. Variety is good (random 40% spot subsets, Decoy, House Rules). But the round is cut into 4 phases and only about 1:30 of a 5-minute round is the actual fun core. The Parent, the star role, spends 1:45 in a generic lane-dodge mini-game that has nothing to do with the house, so their first 30 s is Subway-Surfers filler. PANIC is so assisted (tap mess, tap the glowing arrow on one of 2-3 lit spots) that hiding takes no skill or creativity, which hurts the 'Most Ridiculous Hiding Spot' payoff. A first-time Parent gets only Sniff, so new Parents are weak and boring to play against. If the Parent leaves, the round dies (an AI Parent exists only in practice). Smashing gives an immediate thrill in the first 30 s, but it's shallow points-farming.
R3-01.fix: Replace the drive with the Parent present from the start (e.g., on a phone call, a limited-view baby-monitor cam, or peeking through windows from the yard) so the cat-and-mouse runs all round. Let PANIC hiding be freeform: carry the item anywhere, and fits are judged by size, with no arrow prompts after onboarding. Give new Parents 2 gadgets. Add an AI Parent takeover when the Parent leaves.

R3-02.why: Drawing runes feels good to touch immediately, misfires (rubber chicken, stolen hat) make failure funny, and relics that change fusion behaviour give roguelite build depth. Simultaneous-cast fusion is a real teamwork verb that works without voice. Problems: (1) Fusions are the headline and enemies REQUIRE them, but the game supports 1-4 players. Solo players and teams that don't coordinate can't reach the core hook and hit an enemy wall. (2) The 'suggested partner rune' icon turns fusion into Simon Says: you discover nothing and make no decision. (3) There's no movement or camera, only balcony hops, so it's a static turret game and the spatial play is thin. (4) 6 runes drawn hundreds of times per session become repetitive. Server-side classification adds latency to every cast, and when the classifier misreads a careful trace it feels unfair, not funny. (5) PC mouse-drawing is weaker, and on console the gesture is replaced by a radial menu, which removes the hook entirely.
R3-02.fix: Let a single player fuse by chaining 2 runes within the window (a teammate fusion gives a bigger version). Remove partner-rune suggestions after the first run so the Rune Book is something you discover. Classify on the client for instant feedback, with a server check after. Add positional play: balcony choice affects which lanes and enemies you can hit, and a fusion's area depends on where both casters stand.

R3-03.why: It has the cleanest core verb of the set: release-to-freeze is physical, readable comedy with instant tension in the first 30 s, and it plays well with strangers and no voice. The Guard makes real decisions: battery economy, wrong-tag cost, and reading shimmers against NPC statues that drift. Pranks give statues a reason to take risks rather than just hide, and hidden or live prank rotation plus wing lockdown keeps rounds varied and building to a climax. Tagged players stay in through Cracked distractions and revive. Getting caught mid-moustache is funny, not frustrating. Concerns: the LIGHT COMING vignette plus auto-snap posing over-assists the statues, so you stop watching the Guard and skill disappears. Off-plinth auto-snap may be an obvious tell, or else invisible, and both hurt fairness. Lock-on tagging lowers Guard skill. One museum and 8 pranks will get stale over long sessions without new pranks every week. It's a 1-vs-many balance risk, but beam-only tagging is a good limiter.
R3-03.fix: Show the vignette only in onboarding or low ranks, and make reading the Guard yourself the skill. Let players pick between 2-3 freeze poses (quick-tap), with bonus Mischief for poses that match a nearby NPC. Make prank chains interact (cuckoo clock pulls the Guard -> painting swap window). Give the Guard an AI fallback when the Guard leaves.

R3-04.why: With friends, the first 30 s is funny: the raft spins and someone gets blamed. But each player's input is one HOLD button, diluted to 1/6 of the raft's heading. A combined heading arrow plus a ghost 'paddle now' prompt over-assists, so the optimal play is to follow the prompt, which removes most of the coordination puzzle that is the whole joke. Roles add some texture: the Lookout is the one with decisions, the Bailer and Bonker are minor. With random strangers, a troll or AFK seat sinks everyone, and the blame card can turn toxic. Leavers leave dead paddles. Versus (bailing into rivals, balloons, bumping) and the Saboteur Seat are the most interesting parts, but they're layered on a thin base verb. The novelty spike resembles Fart Together and Boat Together, whose ~2K peak suggests the fun wears off fast over long sessions.
R3-04.fix: Give each seat 2 inputs (paddle forward/back, or stroke strength via hold duration) so a single seat can recover a bad heading. Remove the ghost 'paddle now' arrow after onboarding, and make the Lookout the only source of guidance so roles depend on each other. Have AI take empty seats, and auto-kick idlers into AI. Make Versus the default mode with interaction between rafts at every segment.

R3-05.why: The moment-to-moment verbs are satisfying without any progression: the PowerWash-style sweep on drag gives instant tactile reward. It has the richest set of mechanical interactions here: water on grease flares up, breaker before electrical, tank-and-hydrant resource management, critters that hide, flee and wriggle loose if you run, 2-player critters, collapsing floors, dragging downed teammates. Those create real decisions about what to do next, with Overcooked-style triage. It works solo and with strangers because goals are aligned and there's no betrayal toxicity. Failure is designed to be comedic (goat eats the hose). Concerns: generous hose magnetism removes aiming skill, launch has one building type, and a coarse fire grid may make runs feel same-y over long sessions. Rare-critter performance gates risk turning the game into a collection checklist. A critter dying in a fire may feel sad, not funny, for young players.
R3-05.fix: Make fire spread more dynamic and readable (draughts from opened doors, backdraft when you open a hot room) so routing decisions matter. Reduce magnetism at higher alarm tiers. Ship 2 building layouts with strong procedural variation. Make critter failure comedic and never lethal (they flee outside sooty and grumpy) so the stakes are score, not sadness.

overall_notes: No concept is fundamentally boring, so no vetoes. But no concept reaches top-quartile fun (8+) either. A recurring flaw across the round is over-assisted controls: arrow-to-spot hiding, LIGHT COMING warnings, suggested partner runes, ghost paddle prompts. These remove the skill and discovery that make these genres fun. Strongest core loops: R3-03 Statue Shuffle (cleanest tension verb, best with strangers) and R3-05 Blaze Brigade (richest system interactions, best solo/co-op). R3-01 has a great hunt hidden inside a phase structure that sidelines the Parent. R3-02's fusion hook is unavailable to solo players and is reduced to prompts. R3-04 is the thinnest per-player verb and most fragile with strangers and leavers. Every 1vN concept needs an AI takeover when the solo role leaves.
